description: Shared verbatim script for on-screen narration, speech, captions, and transcript.
cues: Each token leaves behind two vectors: a key and a value. One attention head is shown here.
Decoding appends another key–value pair. The earlier vectors stay in the cache.
The next query reuses this growing cache to compute attention over the available context.
Suppose each request reserves twelve token slots, even though its final length is unknown.
Cut the cache into blocks of four. Allocate only the blocks needed by the current tokens.
The same fourteen tokens now occupy twenty slots. Only the final block of each request has slack.
A block table connects the token sequence to physical memory. Matching colors follow the same data.
For token six, divide by the block size. The quotient chooses a block; the remainder chooses a slot.
Follow table[1] to physical block P2, then read slot 2. The logical token index is still six.
The query compares with every valid key, even when those keys are stored in different physical blocks.
Softmax normalizes all of these scores together. Physical block boundaries do not split the denominator.
Use these weights to mix the value vectors. Paging changes storage, while preserving the attention calculation.
At six tokens, the request owns two blocks. Appending token six writes into an existing slot.
Token seven fills the remaining slot. The block table is unchanged.
For token eight, the offset becomes zero. Allocate a free block, then extend the table.
After the request finishes, its unshared blocks return to the pool and can serve another request.
Two continuations can share prefix blocks. Reference counts record how many requests still need each block.
A is about to append into a shared partial block. First copy that block; then change only A’s table.
Now A can write token six into its private copy. B’s data stays unchanged, and the full prefix remains shared.
PagedAttention keeps token order intact while making GPU memory easier to allocate, reuse, and share.
